191.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out.”
191.explanation: The opening lecture of the Uttarādhyayana compares the talkative, unruly pupil to a mangy dog that is chased away from every door.
191.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who keeps up useless talk until his listeners are sick of him ends up scorned by everyone, and the Jain simile shows the talkative pupil driven out wherever he goes.
191._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit for the social rejection of the talker, though the Jain verse lumps talkativeness together with insubordination in a monastic setting.

192.quote_or_event: “A monk should not tell stories, nor ask idle questions, nor gossip. But, knowing the highest Law, he should perform his religious duties, and regard nothing his own.”
192.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga tells the monk to give up story-telling, idle questions and gossip and to spend himself on his religious duties instead.
192.tie_back: Valluvar ranks pointless talk before many people as worse than unkindness to friends, and the Jain rule likewise treats idle talk and gossip as a real fault to be given up, not a harmless habit.
192._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi marks the word for 'gossip' as uncertain); it condemns idle talk, but it does not make the Kural's comparison with wronging friends or mention speaking before a crowd.

193.quote_or_event: “Indulging in meaningless and unrestrained talk out of self-importance is maukharya.”
193.explanation: Pūjyapāda's commentary defines maukharya (garrulity), which Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.32 lists as a lapse in the layperson's vow to avoid purposeless harm (anarthadaṇḍa-virati).
193.tie_back: Valluvar says long talk about worthless things itself announces the speaker's lack of goodness, and Jain lay ethics names that very habit, meaningless talk born of self-importance, as a breach of a vow.
193.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.32, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
193._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a close fit, as 'purposeless' (anartha) matches the Kural's payanila, though the definition comes from Pūjyapāda's commentary and not from Umāsvāti's sūtra itself.

194.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
194.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana puts meaningless speech in the same forbidden class as sinful and hurtful speech, whatever the speaker's motive.
194.tie_back: Valluvar says useless, graceless words cut a person off from virtue, and the Jain rule likewise treats meaningless speech as a moral fault on a level with sinful and hurtful words.
194._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good fit for meaningless speech as a moral fault, but it is a rule and does not describe the speaker being pulled away from goodness.

195.quote_or_event: “When a monk quarrels and uses very bad language, he will suffer great spiritual loss; therefore a wise man should not quarrel.”
195.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that even a monk who has taken the vows loses much of his spiritual gain through careless, bad speech.
195.tie_back: Valluvar warns that even people of fine character lose their excellence and honour if they speak empty words, and the Jain verse likewise says a monk's own words can cost him great spiritual loss.
195._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial, next-best match, since the verse is about quarrelling and abusive language rather than empty talk, though it shares the idea that even the virtuous fall through speech.

196.quote_or_event: “He who is ignorant of the truth, egoistical, greedy, without self-discipline, and who talks loosely, is called ill-behaved and void of learning.”
196.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana counts loose talk among the marks that strip a monk of the name of a disciplined and learned person.
196.tie_back: Valluvar refuses to call the man who parades empty words a real man and calls him chaff, and the Jain text likewise denies the loose talker the standing of a disciplined, learned person.
196._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable but partial fit, since loose talk is one fault among several and the Jain text has nothing like the Kural's striking 'chaff' image.

197.quote_or_event: “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
197.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that a teacher's harsh but useful words are a real benefit to the wise, even if fools resent them.
197.tie_back: Valluvar allows the worthy to say unpleasant things if they must but never useless ones, and the Jain text values rough words that do real good over pleasant ones that do none.
197._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable fit for 'unpleasant but beneficial' speech, though it is told from the listener's side and does not set this against useless talk.

198.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
198.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana joins restraint in speech with the pursuit of valuable knowledge and the avoidance of what is worthless.
198.tie_back: Valluvar says the wise who seek rare benefits never speak words without great benefit, and the Jain verse likewise pairs holding back talk with seeking what is valuable and leaving the worthless aside.
198._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable fit, though 'valuable' and 'worthless' here refer mainly to knowledge, not to the words one speaks.

199.quote_or_event: “Possessing perfect wisdom, a sage always vanquishes (his passions); he correctly expounds the Law; he never neglects even the smallest (duty); he is neither angry nor proud.”
199.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga describes the sage of perfect wisdom as one whose teaching is always correct and who never slips even in the smallest duty.
199.tie_back: Valluvar says those whose vision is free of delusion never speak meaningless words, even by a slip, and the Jain sage of perfect wisdom likewise speaks the Law correctly and never neglects even the smallest duty.
199._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match, since it links perfect wisdom with flawless conduct and right teaching but says nothing specific about meaningless or careless speech.

200.quote_or_event: “Well considering (what one is to say), speaking with precision, one should employ language in moderation and restraint.”
200.explanation: The Ācārāṅga's lecture on modes of speech requires that every word be thought over first and spoken precisely, sparingly and with restraint.
200.tie_back: Valluvar closes the chapter with the rule to speak only useful words and never useless ones, and the Ācārāṅga sets out the same rule for monks: think first, then speak precisely, sparingly and with restraint.
200.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
200._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong thematic fit for disciplined, purposeful speech, though in context the passage is mainly about precision of grammar and assertion rather than usefulness as such.
